html:
Command setup and Working Context

Supported Shell commands can leave verified setup facts for later work in the same conversation: a repository root, an SSH endpoint and host key, a Kubernetes context and namespace, or a SLURM cluster configuration. These records reduce repeated setup discovery. They do not retain a live connection, prove current remote state, grant permissions or make a failed command safe to repeat.

Working Context storage and inheritance owns the shared record limits, conversation scope, projection and recovery rules. This page describes how command adapters obtain and invalidate those facts. Use execution and receipts for authorization and process outcomes.

Request and receipt ownership

flowchart LR S[Shell tool invocation] --> P[Controller adapter prepares private plan] P --> E[Shell executor and Gateway transport] E --> G[Gateway observes setup around requested work] G --> R[Completion receipt] R --> V[Controller validates receipt and provenance] V --> W[Working Context updates verified or stale records] W --> M[Bounded hints for later model requests]

The shared Shell tool calls each adapter's prepare before execution and after_result after execution. The Shell executor collects private setup receipts from completion events. They are separate from ordinary stdout and stderr; adapters do not infer setup by reading command prose. The Gateway service owns buffered/streaming dispatch and invokes the appropriate observer. Observation never dispatches the original command a second time.

Domain Controller owner Gateway owner Retained meaning
Git git.py git_context.py Repository filesystem identity, native paths and a bounded remote configuration manifest.
SSH ssh.py ssh_context.py Authenticated endpoint/account and verified public host key.
Kubernetes kubernetes.py kubernetes_context.py Selected context/namespace and public routing/trust configuration fingerprints.
SLURM slurm.py slurm_context.py Local cluster routing and display configuration identity.

Each adapter validates its record and binds it to the selected Gateway identity. The skill catalog registers these as Working Context adapters, without creating separate domain skills. Runtime guidance comes from the sealed prompt catalog; these folder guides are navigation material.

Git: local metadata, fresh commands

The controller recognizes a bounded set of direct Git operations and derives candidate paths from supported -C, init and clone forms. Shell wrappers, ambiguous destinations, unknown aliases and unsupported global overrides decline new setup discovery. Known verified roots can still be checked alongside another eligible captured command.

The Gateway walks at most 64 ancestors, handles worktrees, gitfiles and bare repositories, and reads bounded configuration files without launching Git. It does not read branch, HEAD contents, status, conflicts or ahead/behind state. Configuration includes and uncertain system defaults cannot establish a complete supported observation. URL rewriting or an oversized remote manifest yields no usable remote subset; the receipt explicitly marks remote information incomplete.

Filesystem/configuration fingerprints detect the supported changes and allow unchanged metadata reuse. They are not a content snapshot or a filesystem lock. The shared file reader checks its open descriptor before and after a bounded read; it follows symlinks and does not independently pin every pathname. Git adds its own configuration metadata recheck. A recreated repository keeps the old identity as stale evidence. Later commands must still obtain fresh Git state and normal execution authorization. Accepted remote URLs remain literal metadata; the adapter's compatibility secrets argument does not perform URL redaction.

SSH: verified host identity without a session

Supported observation uses a direct POSIX OpenSSH invocation with a remote command and a small option subset. It uses strict host checking, batch authentication and no multiplexed connection reuse. Initial enrollment relies on existing OpenSSH trust and actual authentication evidence from a private DEBUG1 log. A bounded post-command ssh -G check declines unsupported proxy routing; no keyscan or automatic trust enrollment occurs.

Reuse supplies the retained public host key through an ephemeral known-hosts file. Stale keys remain pinned until explicitly forgotten and re-enrolled through the normal trust path. Host identity, authentication and configuration failures can stale matching setup; a network outage alone does not replace it. Public projection omits raw key material. The configuration revision fingerprints the selected public mapping, not every byte of SSH configuration.

Temporary logs and pins belong to one invocation and are removed on context exit. Unknown log formats cannot establish setup. Recognized SSH transport failures with exit code 255 replace stderr with a canonical error line; an authenticated remote program that itself exits 255 is a different outcome.

Remote privilege

ssh_privilege.py requires one verified target/account and rechecks the effective configuration after any approval delay. It pins the connection, disables unsupported routing/forwarding behavior and sends the optional sudo password on stdin, never in argv or environment. Gateway-local elevation is a separate execution path.

The remote wrapper emits distinct elevated-start and completion markers. A local SSH process spawn alone does not prove elevated work started. Wrapper/credential material is filtered from bounded output. Missing or inconsistent completion evidence can leave remote effects unknown; the implementation preserves that fact without automatic retry. Shared resource admission and Gateway recovery own persistence; the wrapper does not add a synchronous disk checkpoint for each marker. The target-integrity report retains the original implementation and acceptance evidence.

Kubernetes: configuration identity, not object memory

The Gateway supports one selected kubeconfig, safe YAML bounded to 512 KiB, 20,000 nodes and depth 24, and up to 128 KiB of public CA data. It rejects aliases, duplicate keys, ambiguous config lists, explicit proxy routes, insecure TLS and impersonation. Relative CA paths use the kubeconfig's lexical directory, including when the config itself is a symlink. Certificate fingerprints include only public X.509 certificates. Credentials and exec-plugin details remain owned by kubectl; the observer does not run an authentication plugin or contact a cluster.

Publication requires equal nonempty setup before and after an explicitly executed, successful command whose supported syntax is eligible for cluster contact. That syntax flag is not independent proof of a network request. The controller also checks Gateway identity, selectors, receipt shape and execution truth before upserting a record. Different namespaces can coexist; changed trust or cluster identity leaves older evidence stale. Configuration or credential failures cannot justify reusing old pod contents or bypassing RBAC. Windows command recognition is narrow and declines ambiguous quoting or native argument forms.

SLURM: local routing identity

Linux observation recognizes supported direct reads through squeue, sinfo, scontrol and sdiag. It excludes job submission, mutations, interactive commands, federation ambiguity and unsupported selectors. The observer reads SLURM_CONF or the single supported default /etc/slurm/slurm.conf; it does not search alternate locations or fetch configless configuration. A competing /etc/slurm.conf makes the default ambiguous.

Configuration reads allow at most 128 KiB per file, 512 KiB total, 16 files, four include levels and 16 controllers. Unsupported continuations, cycles, duplicate identity keys and ambiguous relative includes decline setup. Authentication paths are not followed; only selected configuration/display environment values are read. No queue data, scheduler credential or remote-controller authentication is retained.

Equal before/after configuration and truthful successful local-cluster execution are required for publication. Independent Gateway routes can coexist. Expected missing/malformed configuration leaves ordinary Shell available. Structural runtime defects have a distinct path: before dispatch they produce a failed-to-start receipt; after dispatch they preserve the actual process outcome and enter the controller's existing runtime-fault handling. They never cause a replay.

Validation and troubleshooting

If setup is absent, inspect the actual command outcome and the supported command, platform and configuration boundaries above. An unsupported observation does not establish that the external tool or target is unavailable. If setup is stale, obtain fresh authorized evidence; do not infer success from the old record or silently accept a changed SSH host key.

Focused fixtures use temporary Git repositories, loopback OpenSSH with isolated keys and fake sudo, and independent fake Kubernetes/SLURM CLIs through the real Gateway service. See Git, SSH, remote privilege, Kubernetes and SLURM. These fixtures verify the exercised contracts without certifying every external CLI version or live cluster.
